1What statistics is: populations and samples

Math 2260. Probability and Statistics for Science and Engineering.

Definition Textbook definition

Statistics is the science of conducting studies to collect, organize, summarize, analyze, and draw conclusions from data.

Typed note included in the PDF Aran’s typed notes under the photo

Population could be the people taking a test, the score, the people who wrote the exam.

Definition

Population: the group of all subjects being subjects being considered in a study

Sample: a sample is a subject of the population.

The way you gather your sample matters.

We will assume we have simple random samples in this course.

To have a simple random sample, you need to have used a sampling technique with the property that all samples of a given size are equally likely to be selected.

✎ Explanation (added)

Two slips in the typed lines, kept above exactly as typed: “being subjects” is repeated in the population line, and a sample is a subset of the population (a part of it), not a “subject”. Clean versions: a population is the group of all subjects being considered in a study; a sample is a subset of the population.

The first typed line is making a real point: the “subjects” do not have to be people. If the study is about exam scores, the population can be thought of as the set of all the scores. What matters is that the population is everything the study is about, and the sample is the part you actually observe.

Textbook · Devore — population, sample and census: §1.1, p. 3. Devore’s wording for a sample is “a subset of the population”.

2Sampling techniques

Typed note included in the PDF Simple random sample (SRS)

The definition he wrote is the exact one, and the precise wording matters:

every possible sample of size has an equal chance of being selected

Not “every individual has an equal chance.” That’s a weaker condition and a classic exam trap.

✎ Explanation (added)

Why the two wordings are different: suppose a class has 10 men and 10 women and you flip one coin, taking all the men on heads and all the women on tails. Every individual has a 50% chance of being chosen, but most samples of size 10 (any mixed group) can never be chosen. So it is not a simple random sample. In an SRS, every one of the possible groups of 10 is equally likely.

Typed note included in the PDF Aran’s typed note

Other sampling techniques

1) Census: The sample is the population with a census, any property or characteristic you note about the sample immediately carries over to the whole population

✎ Explanation (added)

A census measures everyone, so there is nothing left to infer. It is usually too expensive or impossible, which is why the other techniques exist.

Textbook · Devore — simple random sample (“any particular subset of the specified size has the same chance of being selected”), stratified sampling and convenience samples: §1.1, p. 10. Cluster, multistage and systematic sampling are not covered in Chapters 1–2.

Typed note included in the PDF Stratified sampling

Split the population into strata — groups that are internally similar on something relevant. Then take a random sample from every stratum.

Example: Douglas College students split by faculty (Science, Business, Arts, Health). Randomly pick 25 from each.

Why do it: guarantees every subgroup shows up. Reduces variability if the strata actually differ from each other.

Key phrase to spot on an exam: “divided into groups, sampled from all groups.”

Typed note included in the PDF Cluster sampling

Split the population into clusters — groups that each ideally look like a mini version of the whole population. Then randomly pick a few clusters and take everyone in the selected clusters.

Example: number all 120 sections of first-year courses, randomly pick 8 sections, survey every student in those 8.

Why do it: cheap and logistically easy. You only travel to 8 places, not 120.

Key phrase: “sampled from some groups, took everyone in those.”

Typed note included in the PDF Stratified vs. cluster — the confusion point
Groups are…You sample…
Stratifiedsimilar WITHIN, different BETWEENfrom EVERY group (a few from each)
Clustermixed WITHIN, similar BETWEENfrom a FEW groups (all of each)

Mnemonic: Stratified = Some from all. Cluster = all from some.

Try it — see each sampling technique pick its sample

A population of 120 people arranged in 6 groups of 20. Pick a technique, then press “Draw again” a few times and watch which people can end up in the sample.

Interactive widget: open the page on a screen to use it.
Typed note included in the PDF Multistage sampling

Exactly what it sounds like: you combine methods across several stages, narrowing down each time. Used when the population is huge and you have no master list of individuals.

Classic textbook example — a national survey:

Stage 1:randomly select 10 provinces/regions(cluster)
Stage 2:within each, randomly select 5 cities(cluster)
Stage 3:within each city, split into income brackets, randomly pick households(stratified)
Stage 4:within each household, randomly pick one adult(SRS)

Why it exists: nobody has a list of all 30 million Canadian adults. But you do have a list of provinces, and each province has a list of cities, and so on. You only need a full list at the final stage, for the few units you actually selected.

Statistics Canada and Gallup polls work this way. Your prof will likely say “real-world large surveys are almost always multistage.”

Typed note included in the PDF Systematic sampling — the mechanics

Population size , desired sample size .

Step 1:   (round down)
Step 2:randomly pick a start between 1 and
Step 3:take that person, then every -th after

Worked example: students, want .

k = 1000 / 50 = 20
Random start: say 7
Sample: 7, 27, 47, 67, 87, ... , 987

That’s 50 people. The only randomness is in the starting point — once you pick 7, everything else is locked in.

Typed note included in the PDF Convenience sampling

Definition

You take whoever is easiest to reach. No randomization at any point.

Examples:

  • Ask the first 30 people who walk past you in the concourse
  • Post a poll on Instagram and use whoever answers
  • Survey your own class about student opinions
  • Call-in radio polls, restaurant comment cards, online product reviews
Typed note included in the PDF Why it’s on the list

It is not a probability sampling method. Nobody has a known, nonzero chance of being selected. That means:

  • You can’t compute a margin of error
  • Confidence intervals and hypothesis tests are invalid
  • You cannot generalize to the population at all

Every formula in this course assumes random sampling. Convenience sampling breaks the assumption at the root, so no amount of math downstream can repair it.

Typed note included in the PDF “Exam traps” (pasted note, as it appears in the PDF)

Trap 1 — “A sample of 5,000 was collected. Is this reliable?” The size is bait. Ask how it was collected first. Large never fixes a non-random method.

Trap 2 — Identification questions where “random” appears in the wording but nothing was actually randomized. “A reporter randomly approaches shoppers at a mall.” That’s convenience, not SRS. “Randomly” in casual speech ≠ random sampling. The population is only mall shoppers at that hour, and the reporter picks who looks approachable.

Trap 3 — Being asked why it’s invalid. Expected answer: selection probabilities are unknown, so the sample is not representative and no inference to the population is justified.

The screenshot ends here with a “scroll down” arrow, so anything below Trap 3 is not in the PDF.

3Inferential and descriptive statistics

Typed note included in the PDF Inferential

use a SAMPLE to draw conclusions about a POPULATION you didn’t measure; involves uncertainty → probability

Inferential Statistics

This side of statistics deals with observing a property or characteristic of a sample and using it to make statements about the population that is likely to be true.

✱ Use probability theory

Typed note included in the PDF Descriptive

summarize the data you HAVE: mean, median, sd, graphs, tables; no claims beyond the data itself

Typed note included in the PDF Aran’s typed note

Note We will use small data sets in class. In practice, real data sets are usually much larger.

(try to avoid small sample sizes

✎ Explanation (added)

The split to remember: descriptive statistics only describes the data in front of you (a table, a histogram, a mean). Inferential statistics goes further and says something about the whole population from a sample, and because a sample can be unlucky, every such statement comes with a probability attached. That is why the probability chapters come before the inference chapters.

Textbook · Devore — descriptive statistics: §1.1, p. 4. Inferential statistics: pp. 5–6, with Figure 1.2 (p. 6) showing probability going from population to sample and inferential statistics going from sample to population.

Sampling: must be random — this is why he covered sampling first. Inference: back to a claim about the population, with a stated level of uncertainty.

✎ Explanation (added)

Reading the symbols: is a population mean and is a sample mean; is a population standard deviation and a sample standard deviation; is a population proportion and a sample proportion. Greek letters and plain belong to the population. The mean and standard deviation are defined in Lecture 2.

4Types of data: categorical, quantitative, discrete, continuous

Definition

Quantitative Data – Numerical in nature. Values arise from some quantity we can measure or count. There is a meaningful difference between allowable values.

We will consider two types of quantitative variables, discrete and continuous.

✎ Explanation (added)

“A meaningful difference between allowable values” is the test: 7 seeds minus 5 seeds is 2 seeds, which means something. Jersey number 23 minus jersey number 12 is 11, which means nothing, so jersey numbers are not quantitative even though they are written with digits.

Textbook · Devore — discrete and continuous variables: Definition in §1.2, p. 16.

Typed note included in the PDF Categorical (qualitative) data

Definition

Data that places a subject into a category or group. Labels, not measurements. Arithmetic on them is meaningless.

Examples

Eye colourbrown, blue, green, hazel
MajorScience, Business, Arts
Blood typeA, B, AB, O
ProvinceBC, AB, ON, QC
Yes/no responsessmoker / non-smoker
Marital statussingle, married, divorced
Letter gradeA, B, C, D, F
Satisfaction ratingpoor, fair, good, excellent
Jersey number#12, #23, #99
Typed note included in the PDF What you can do with categorical data

Count and take proportions. That’s it.

Blood type of 200 donorsCountProportion
O9045%
A8040%
B2211%
AB84%

Graphs: bar chart, pie chart. Not histogram — that’s for quantitative data, and mixing them up is a marked error later in the course.

Typed note included in the PDF “Exam traps” (pasted note, as it appears in the PDF)

Trap 1 — The numeric-looking categorical variable. “Is a student ID number qualitative or quantitative?” Qualitative. This shows up constantly.

Trap 2 — Zip/postal codes and area codes. Same thing. Always categorical.

Trap 3 — Counting the number of subjects in a category is quantitative, even though the variable itself is categorical. “Eye colour” is categorical; “how many students have brown eyes” is a count, which is quantitative discrete.

The screenshot is cut off partway through the last word (“discrete”).

Textbook · Devore — categorical versus numerical characteristics: §1.1, p. 3. Histograms for qualitative data: §1.2, p. 23, Example 1.13 and Figure 1.13 (pp. 23–24).

Typed note included in the PDF

1. Quantitative (numerical) data — the other half of the split. Actual measurements where arithmetic works: height, weight, income, test score, time.

2. Discrete vs. continuous — the subdivision of quantitative.

  • Discrete = countable, gaps between values. Number of children, cars in a lot, defects per batch.
  • Continuous = any value in an interval, measured not counted. Height, weight, time, temperature.
  • Trap he’ll flag: money. Usually treated as continuous even though it’s technically discrete to the cent.
Example Examples

a) We are looking at the number of children Canadian couples have.

b) The exact height of spruce trees on Vancouver Island

Fragments visible at the cut-off left edge of the photo read “…ties in this course.” and “…no allowable values”. They belong to lines that are mostly outside the frame.

✎ Explanation (added)

The quick test: can you list the possible values with gaps between them (0, 1, 2, …)? Then the variable is discrete, and it usually comes from counting. If between any two possible values there is always another possible value, it is continuous, and it usually comes from measuring. A couple cannot have 1.5 children, but a tree can be 21.37… m tall. So b) is continuous.

5Frequency distributions

A natural thing to do when looking at data sets is to count the number of times each data value occurs, or the number of times data values in a certain interval occur.

Definition

If we recorded these counts in a table, we get a frequency distribution table.

(or frequency table or a frequency distribution or a distribution)

Typed note included in the PDF Frequency distributions

What he’s saying

You have a raw pile of data. First useful move: count how often things occur. Two flavours depending on data type:

  1. Count each distinct value — works when there are few possible values (categorical data, or discrete quantitative with a small range)
  2. Count values falling in an interval — needed when values are all different (continuous data), so you bin them into ranges

Put those counts in a table and you have a frequency distribution table. He listed the synonyms: frequency table, frequency distribution, or just “a distribution.” All the same thing.

Typed note included in the PDF Type 1 — counting each value

Number of siblings for 20 students:

Those ranges are classes. He’s setting up terminology you’ll need next: class limits, class width, class boundaries, midpoints.

✎ Explanation (added)

A relative frequency is the fraction of the data taking that value, so it lets you compare data sets of different sizes. Check: . They must always add to 1 because the frequencies add to and each one was divided by . Later in the course, relative frequencies are how probabilities get estimated.

Textbook · Devore — relative frequency = (number of times the value occurs) ÷ (number of observations): §1.2, p. 16.

If there are lots of different data values, we can use a group frequency distribution table and look at class frequencies.

The class frequencies come from adding the earlier table in pairs: for the class 5–6, for 7–8, and for 9–10. Still . Grouping loses detail (you can no longer tell how many apples had exactly 7 seeds) in exchange for a shorter table.

✱ If you use this notation (the table as written, with an arrow to it), data values on a class boundary go in the class with larger values.

At the right edge of the board, cut off by the photo: a small number line marked at 12.5, and “← can also use … frequencies”.

✎ Explanation (added)

The table as first written has 14.0 at the end of one class and the start of the next, so a plant that is exactly 14.0 cm could be counted twice. The rule fixes that: a value on a boundary goes up, into the class with larger values. The bracket notation says the same thing with symbols: means .

Every class here has the same class width, cm. The cut-off remark on the right is almost certainly “can also use relative frequencies”: dividing each count by 20 gives 0.20, 0.25, 0.30, 0.15, 0.10, which again add to 1.

Textbook · Devore — class intervals for continuous data and the “–<” notation, so that a boundary value falls in the class with larger values: §1.2, pp. 18–19, Example 1.10 and Figure 1.8.

Dot plot

✎ Explanation (added)

A dot plot is the frequency table turned on its side: the height of each stack is the frequency. It only works well when values repeat, which is why it suits discrete data with a small range.

Textbook · Devore — dotplots: §1.2, pp. 15–16, Example 1.8 and Figure 1.6.

Histogram / Bar chart:

↑ If we use relative frequencies instead of frequencies, all that changes is the scale used on the vertical axis. The shape of the histogram does not change.

Try it — frequency or relative frequency, single values or classes

Switch the vertical scale and watch that the bars keep exactly the same shape. Then switch to classes of width 2 to get the grouped table from the board (5–6, 7–8, 9–10).

Interactive widget: open the page on a screen to use it.
✎ Explanation (added)

Why the shape cannot change: every bar height is divided by the same number, . The tallest bar goes from 3 to 0.3, the shortest from 1 to 0.1, so all the ratios between bars stay the same. Only the labels on the vertical axis change.

Textbook · Devore — histogram for discrete data (a rectangle centred on each value, height = relative frequency): §1.2, p. 17, and Figure 1.7 (p. 18).

Two differences from the seed histogram. First, the bars are drawn over intervals (12.5 to 14, 14 to 15.5, …) instead of being centred on single values, because any height in the interval is possible. Second, the bars touch, because the classes share boundaries and leave no gaps. Try it first, then open the worked answer

a. A probability question starts from an assumed population and asks about the sample. For example: if 20% of all such computers need warranty service, what is the probability that more than 25 of the 100 sampled computers do? Or that between 15 and 25 do? Or that none do?

b. An inferential question runs the other way, from the observed sample to the population. For example: 100 computers are sampled and 15 need warranty service. What does that say about the proportion of all computers of this brand and model that need service, and how confident can we be that this proportion is below 20%?

This is exactly the down arrow (sampling, probability) and the up arrow (inference) in the “core structure” diagram, and in Devore’s Figure 1.2 on p. 6.

8Lecture at a glance

Population and sample

Population: all subjects in the study. Sample: a subset of it.

Simple random sample

Every possible sample of size is equally likely to be selected.

Sampling techniques

Census · SRS · stratified (some from all groups) · cluster (all from some groups) · multistage · systematic (every -th) · convenience (bad).

Systematic step
Two sides of statistics

Descriptive: summarize the data you have. Inferential: use a sample to make statements about the population, using probability.

Parameter vs statistic
Types of data

Categorical (labels) or quantitative (numbers). Quantitative is discrete (gaps, counted) or continuous (an interval, measured).

Relative frequency

They sum to 1.

Class boundaries

A value on a boundary goes in the class with larger values.

Histogram

Discrete: bars centred on each value. Continuous: bars over class intervals, touching. Changing to relative frequency only rescales the vertical axis.

What a typical exam question looks like
  • A short description of how a sample was collected (“the students in 8 randomly chosen sections were all surveyed”) and the question: which sampling technique is this? Be ready to tell stratified from cluster and systematic from simple random.
  • State the definition of a simple random sample, a population, a sample, a parameter or a statistic, in the instructor’s wording.
  • Classify a variable as categorical or quantitative, and if quantitative as discrete or continuous (number of children, height of a tree, postal code, student number).
  • Given a small data set, build the frequency table and the relative frequency table, and confirm the relative frequencies sum to 1.
  • Given grouped data, say which class a boundary value belongs to and rewrite the classes in notation.
  • Draw a dot plot or a histogram from a frequency table with a title, labelled axes and a sensible scale, and say what changes if relative frequencies are used.
